title: The Death of an AI Playbook
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Nick Potkalitsky tracks what happened to New York City's ambitious March AI policy, once the most comprehensive K-12 AI framework in the country, after its promised follow-up "AI Playbook" quietly never shipped and the whole document disappeared, replaced by a shorter family-facing guidance that reclassifies AI use as a subset of screen time. He reads this substitution as revealing, not incidental: a red/yellow/green risk-tiered governance approach for AI failed because AI use slips between risk categories in practice, so the district switched to governing something it actually can measure, minutes of screen exposure, rather than the thing it cannot, whether a given use builds or bypasses a student's thinking. Potkalitsky argues this is fundamentally a story about ungovernability rather than a developmental maturation of policy, since the object (AI) is changing faster than any playbook or layperson's understanding can track. He closes by warning that banning AI in school does not remove it from students' lives, it just relocates its ungoverned use off-campus, comparing this to letting kids ride 40-mph motorized bikes unsupervised while the official driving curriculum only begins at sixteen.
points: Potkalitsky's central claim is a substitution, not a maturation: NYC didn't refine its AI governance, it swapped an ungovernable object (AI's cognitive effects) for a governable proxy (screen-time minutes), which is why the promised 'AI Playbook' never had to ship.

He distinguishes reactivity (responding to external political/legal pressure) from responsivity (responding to the object itself) and shows the distinction collapses for AI specifically, because the technology changes faster than any policy document or layperson's understanding can track.

The prohibition-offloads-supervision argument is his sharpest point: banning AI in school doesn't remove students from AI, it just moves unsupervised use off-campus while delaying formal AI literacy instruction to 'two 45-minute modules' years after first use.

The motorized-bike analogy crystallizes his critique of sequencing: students are already using powerful, fast-moving tools unsupervised while the official curriculum treats readiness as something to address only much later, mirroring how driver's ed arrives at 16 regardless of when kids start riding.
quotes: The March framework attempted to govern AI through a Traffic Light. Red, yellow, and green sorted uses by risk, an arrangement familiar from over a decade of technology policy. A red/yellow/green scheme focuses on access control. Who can use AI? When can you use it? But AI quickly slips between categories in actual use.

In March, AI was treated as a novel governance object requiring its own dedicated apparatus. In September, it is folded into a screen-time policy and governed by the same developmental logic that districts are applying to cell phones and tablets.

In effect, prohibition just offloads the complexities of AI into off-campus spaces. It removes supervision and guidance, and leaves unsupervised use in place, calling on parents to do the real work of AI literacy. This is the irony. Parents calling for bans of technology in school are creating more work for themselves.

In a somewhat stretched analogy: my neighborhood is now host to packs of elementary and middle school students riding motorized bicycles that hit 40 miles per hour, but our current system asks them to become proficient at driving only when they turn 16.

Screen time is (sort of) governable. Minutes can be counted. Devices can be closed. AI and its impact on learning cannot so easily be counted or closed down. The policy governs the thing it can measure and sets aside the thing that cannot.
The children on those motorized bikes are not waiting for a license. They are already in traffic.
